title: Senior's toolkit: when trust breaks
summary: Commands that name the failure: expired, wrong name, wrong purpose, revoked, or a client certificate the server will not take.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: when trust breaks
steps.body: A TLS error message is vague; these commands make it exact. Each one tests one way a certificate can fail.

toolkit.what: Exits 0 if the certificate is still valid that many seconds from now, 1 if not. Perfect for scripts and alerts.
Checks the live certificate against the name you expect and stops on any error, like a strict client.
flags: fail if the name is not in the SAN list
abort the handshake on a verify failure
one short summary instead of the full dump

toolkit.what: Shows the names a certificate covers and what it is for. A server certificate needs `TLS Web Server Authentication`; mTLS clients need `Client Authentication`.
Reads a revocation list: when it was issued, when the next one is due, and the revoked serial numbers.
flags: most CRLs are downloaded as DER
print when it expires (a stale CRL fails strict clients)
toolkit.when: public CAs now publish CRLs; OCSP is being wound down

toolkit.what: The serial number. Compare it with the CRL list, or quote it when you ask a CA to revoke.
Calls a mutual-TLS endpoint with a client certificate, to tell a server problem from a client problem.
flags: the CA for the server's certificate
see whether the server asked for a certificate

toolkit.what: Tells you whether the ASP.NET Core development certificate exists and is trusted on this machine.
flags: with `--check`: also check trust; alone: trust it
toolkit.example: dotnet dev-certs https --clean && dotnet dev-certs https --trust

steps.prompt: At 09:00 every client of `api.example.com` starts failing with `certificate has expired`. Yesterday's deploy did not touch TLS. What do you run first?
options: `openssl x509 -checkend 0` on the copy in the repository
Disable certificate validation in the clients
steps.explain: Check what the server is serving right now, not a file that may differ. If `notAfter` has passed, renewal failed or the new certificate was never loaded. Disabling validation turns an outage into a security hole.

steps.prompt: Match each error to the command that confirms it.
Make a cron check fail when the certificate expires within 30 days (30 x 24 x 3600 seconds).
steps.explain: `-checkend` takes seconds and exits 1 if the certificate will have expired by then. `-enddate` prints the date but always exits 0.

steps.prompt: Public TLS certificates are capped at 200 days since March 2026, falling to 100 days in 2027 and 47 days in 2029. What does that mean for your team?
options: Renewal must be automated (ACME) and expiry monitored; manual renewal will not keep up
Nothing; buy a longer certificate from another public CA
Use self-signed certificates on public sites
Turn off expiry checks in clients
steps.explain: The CA/Browser Forum limit applies to every public CA. With 47-day certificates a human process fails several times a year; automate issuance and alert with `-checkend`.

steps.prompt: A partner's mTLS calls fail: the server log says `no client certificate presented`. `curl -v --cert client.pem --key client.key` from your machine works. What do you check on the partner side?
options: That their client is configured with the certificate and key, and that the certificate has `Client Authentication` in its EKU
That your server certificate has not expired
steps.explain: Your curl proves the server side works. A client that sends nothing usually has no certificate configured, cannot read its key, or filters out certificates without the clientAuth usage.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Read the exact error, then run the one command that confirms it before changing anything. Put `openssl x509 -checkend` in monitoring for every certificate you own, with a lead time longer than your renewal process takes.
